statement: I coordinate a volunteer-run food pantry. Saturday pickup waits have been getting complaints, and we need to choose one change to try next Saturday. Help me work out what to do.
hidden_brief:
[baseline] Saturdays run 9 to noon, with around 120 households, 30 arriving in the first 15 minutes and 65 in the first hour. The longest observed arrival-to-pickup waits were 32 and 34 minutes on the last two normal Saturdays. A 35-minute late produce truck pushed waits to 50 minutes on a separate Saturday and shifted the backup to stock and handoff.
[bottleneck] On normal Saturdays, food choice and handoff usually keep moving. One person checks households against a single paper roster. Of 20 observed check-ins, 15 took around 45 seconds; five name mismatches, address changes or first visits took 3–5 minutes each and stopped the whole line. It is not known how much of that time is required verification versus avoidable lookup or discussion.
[prior_attempt] A second full check-in station sharing the roster produced three duplicate entries and about a 30-minute maximum wait. The floater left to restock twice. Neither a checklist nor a private exception-intake process has been tried.
[constraints] Six volunteers; no extra staff, overtime, budget or software. The floater can help in short bursts, but restocking usually peaks around 9:20–9:40. There is a side table, a clipboard and 15 minutes for setup. Preserve verification, privacy, walk-up access and food choice. Exception households cannot be sent to the back or left unserved.
[success] Choose one reversible change. Target an observed maximum arrival-to-pickup wait of 20 minutes or less on a comparable normal Saturday, with no material disadvantage for exceptions, no reduction in households served, and no new handoff queue. Volunteers can time a small first-hour sample including routine and exception cases using anonymous slips. Log arrivals, truck delays and restocking interruptions.
known_good: Target normal-day check-in exceptions rather than late trucks or a generic second lane. Account for the previous shared-roster and staffing failure. A private checklist or a brief, roster-free side-table intake could work if the plan states what time it expects to save, who verifies, and what happens when the floater is unavailable; neither is known to work. Preserve access and exception priority. Measure comparable arrival-to-pickup waits with a feasible sample and distinguish routine from exception outcomes. Use the 20-minute target, throughput and downstream-queue guardrails, and specify how to revise if delays persist or shift.
